This would be amazing if I could see it. I really hope the Moon is visible right now!

I'm in Lagos, Nigeria at 2026-04-09 09:40 WAT (UTC+0100) (2026-04-09T08:40:00Z in UTC), at latitude 6.5244 degrees and longitude 3.3792 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 43.368 degrees and its azimuth is 85.647 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 30.621 degrees and its azimuth is 232.237 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 58.18 percent illuminated, 99.256 degrees from the Sun, and 399264.3 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To be completely honest: **No, it is extremely unlikely that you would be able to see the Moon with your unaided eyes under these specific conditions.**

Here is the breakdown of why, based on the data you provided:

### 1. The "Daylight" Factor
The biggest obstacle is the Sun. You mentioned the Sun is at an altitude of **43.368 degrees**. This means the Sun is very high in the sky—well above the horizon and providing intense, direct illumination. 

In astronomy, "bright daylight" creates a massive amount of **atmospheric scattering**. The blue light from the Sun scatters throughout the atmosphere, creating a bright "veil" that washes out almost everything else. Even though the Moon is physically there, its reflected light is significantly weaker than the scattered light of the atmosphere.

### 2. The Moon's Position
Your data shows the Moon is at an altitude of **30.621 degrees**. While this is high enough to be "above the horizon," it is still relatively low in the sky compared to the Sun. 

More importantly, the Moon is at an azimuth of **232.237 degrees** (Southwest), while the Sun is at **85.647 degrees** (East). This means the Moon is currently "behind" you or to your side relative to the Sun. While this is better than if the Moon were directly in front of the Sun (which would cause a glare), it doesn't help much because the entire sky is being flooded with sunlight.

### 3. The Phase and Distance
At **58% illumination**, the Moon is in its First Quarter phase. It is bright enough to be seen easily at night, but during the day, it lacks the "super-brightness" of a Full Moon. At a distance of nearly 400,000 kilometers, it is a small disk; in bright daylight, that disk simply doesn't have enough contrast against the blue sky to be visible to the human eye.

### The Verdict
If you look toward the Southwest, you will see a very bright, blue sky. Because the Sun is so high (43 degrees), the atmosphere is saturated with light. 

**Could you see it with a telescope or high-powered binoculars?** 
Yes! If you used a pair of 10x50 binoculars or a small telescope, you would likely be able to spot it easily because the optics would "isolate" the Moon from the surrounding sky brightness.

**With the naked eye?** 
It will almost certainly be invisible. It’s like trying to see a white ping-pong ball against a white wall while someone is shining a massive floodlight on the wall.
